name: Yusuf Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the team that maintains login software for a tech company serving schools, and I have a master’s degree. I start with overnight account lockouts and ask support which teachers could not get into a lesson. I like fixing the small fault that stopped a class, but I get uneasy when someone suggests sending real student records to a new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the login team that an AI helper can tidy routine checks, but it cannot decide who should get into a school account. I use one now and then on fake data, and I still read the result line by line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My senior pay is above average and I have more than a year of basic expenses saved. We have several school customers and plenty of other software firms nearby, so a little automation does not threaten my pay this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the login service and ask school support staff for the most common lockout complaint. I’d keep saving 200 a month while the wage holds and compare the helper’s output with our own checks before using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm. An account problem is a nuisance for a teacher, but this small AI change leaves us time to fix it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the last lockout cost someone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A teacher lost the first ten minutes of class while a password reset went to an old email address. I fixed the route, but the support worker had to calm the class first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why fake data in the AI helper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real login record can show where a child studies. I would not paste that into a tool whose storage rules I have not checked.

say: I think **routine AI checks** can help, but a person should decide account access.
I tell colleagues to use **fake data** until storage rules are clear.
think: I have **over a year saved** and higher-than-usual senior pay.
I see **several school customers** and local firms keeping my income secure for now.
do: **Keep leading** the login service and ask support about lockout complaints.
**Save 200 monthly** while wages hold and compare AI output with our checks.
feel: **Calm** about income and time to fix account problems.
S0.quote: A real login record can show where a child studies.
fieldNote: His occasional AI use is limited to **fake data** until storage rules are clear.
Strong savings, **several customers** and local alternatives support a calm baseline.

steps.text: Keep leading the school login service and review access decisions
Save 200 monthly while senior wages continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our engineers the company should show which coding and support tasks AI takes and what happens to the people doing them. I’d ask our staff group for paid training and a clear rule on school data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Automated code and checking could shrink my team, though I think someone still has to investigate a serious login failure. My own role might survive but my hours or pay could change if management says fewer people can cover more schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new AI method for finding why a login fails, using fake records and past incidents. In the first year I’d join the staff group’s meeting on staffing and school data, and ask our manager for a written account of which roles change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, even with savings. I know how to test a tool, but I cannot decide whether the company keeps the same number of engineers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a useful test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d replay the old-email reset fault and see whether the tool finds it without seeing a child’s real details. If it invents a cause, I would put the result back on the shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your team about your worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I would say my pay could change too. I do not want a comfortable senior to ask junior developers to be calm while their jobs are first to go.

say: I want a **staffing account** as AI takes coding and support tasks.
I want our **staff group** to seek paid training and school-data rules.
think: I expect **automated checking** could shrink the login team.
I worry my **hours or pay** could change if fewer engineers cover more schools.
do: **Learn AI fault tracing** on fake login records and past incidents this month.
**Join staff group talks** and request a written list of changing roles.
feel: **Anxious** about pay and staffing despite a strong cushion.
S1.quote: I do not want a comfortable senior to ask junior developers to be calm while their jobs are first to go.
fieldNote: His **new AI test** targets a known login fault without exposing real children’s details.
He names his own **pay risk** as well as junior job losses.

steps.text: Learn AI login fault tracing using fake records and past incidents
Join staff group talks on staffing and school-data rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could do most of the code, checks and plans I now lead. Robots around 2031 may change school buildings, but my screen work faces the earlier date, so staff need a clear timetable now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer role could be cut even with strong performance. Fourteen months of expenses saved lets me refuse a bad offer, but if similar firms automate together, money only delays the choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the staff group now to negotiate notice and company-paid training, and I’d stop planning a year abroad with my partner. If the role ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid school account support and security review jobs only where vacancies exist; I would not quit for an unpaid guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing the job I know. I could keep paying rent for a while, but I would still need a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner Mara that we should keep the travel money until we know whether my job survives. She has her own work, but I do not want our rent resting on it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What salary would make a new role possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would accept less than my current high pay if it still covers my share of rent and basic bills. I would not use savings to hide a permanent shortfall.

say: I want a **worker timetable** for full AGI by 2028.
I see **robots around 2031** as later than the change to my screen work.
think: I expect my **developer role** could be cut despite strong performance.
I know **fourteen months saved** delays, rather than removes, a wage problem.
do: **Seek paid training** and notice terms through our staff group now.
**Pause the year abroad** with Mara to keep the travel money.
**Apply for paid support** if displaced, accepting only offers covering my rent share and bills.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing my known role despite savings.
S2.quote: I would not use savings to hide a permanent shortfall.
fieldNote: He sees the **2028 thinking-work date** as his deadline, while robots follow later.
Strong savings let him **refuse a bad offer**, but he still expects a lost wage.

steps.text: Ask the staff group to negotiate notice and company-paid training
Pause the planned year abroad with Mara and keep travel savings
Apply for paid school account support or security review vacancies after displacement
Accept only offers covering his share of rent and basic bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the company to use five years to test which account decisions still need a person when full AGI arrives in 2031. I’d ask our staff group to check claims about paid transfers, and I would personally test recovery work before asking anyone else to follow me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 2031 thinking date reaches nearly all my job, while robots arrive about 2034 and add little to a login screen. I might move into account recovery work, but AI could take much of that too; I can afford a small course to test my interest without leaving my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d pay 240 from savings for a four-week evening course on recovering locked accounts, then practise with invented accounts at home. I’d keep saving 300 a month if pay holds; after 2031 I’d apply for paid recovery or security review vacancies if they still exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious but less rushed. I can pay for a bounded test without betting my rent on a new profession.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test in that course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d time how long it takes me to verify a locked-out teacher in a practice case, then explain each check in plain words. A 240 course can buy me a test, not a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay for the course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fourteen months saved makes 240 affordable while I still earn my developer wage. I would not spend that cushion on a long unpaid break or claim a course guarantees an opening.

say: I want **account decisions** tested before full AGI reaches our code in 2031.
I would ask our **staff group** to check claims about paid transfers.
think: I face **thinking AI in 2031** rather than the later robot date.
I can afford a **small course** to test recovery work, though AI might change that work too.
do: **Pay 240** for a four-week evening recovery course and practise on invented accounts this month.
**Save 300 monthly** while my developer pay holds.
**Apply for paid recovery** or security vacancies after 2031 only if posts remain.
feel: **Anxious but less rushed** because I can afford a bounded skills test.
S3.quote: A 240 course can buy me a test, not a new career.
fieldNote: His **four-week course** is a 240 self-funded test from strong savings, not a promised job.
He practises on **invented accounts** and keeps the search conditional on actual paid vacancies after 2031.

steps.text: Pay 240 for a four-week evening course on locked-account recovery
Save 300 monthly while developer wages continue
Apply for paid recovery or security vacancies if available after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years is enough to set rules for school data and let workers try new skills before full AGI arrives in 2036. I’d still remind the team that robots for hands-on jobs follow around 2039, after our code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a larger cushion and learn whether I am good at helping people recover accounts. I would test that with a small offline practice site and invented users; no real school records would leave our systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep leading login releases and spend about 120 on guides for building an offline practice site with invented accounts. I’d build and test its recovery steps on weekends, and separately save toward eighteen months of bills while wages hold. If my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid support or security work only where vacancies remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy about the eventual job change, but secure in the next few years. I can test a method on my own time without asking a manager to make room on a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would try your practice site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Hana teaches and could try the recovery instructions on an invented account if she has time. I’d ask where the words confuse her, then rewrite the steps before showing anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the staff group to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our staff group to demand a rule that school login records stay inside approved systems. A child’s account history should not be a practice file for strangers.

I remind colleagues **robots around 2039** follow the earlier thinking-work change.
think: I could build **more savings** and test account recovery on an offline practice site.
I would use **invented accounts**, keeping real school records inside approved systems.
do: **Keep leading releases** and buy about 120 of guides for an offline practice site.
**Build recovery steps** with invented accounts on weekends; separately save toward eighteen months while wages hold.
**Seek paid support** only if my developer job ends after 2036 and vacancies remain.
feel: **Uneasy about 2036**, but secure while I test recovery work on my own time.
S4.quote: A child’s account history should not be a practice file for strangers.
fieldNote: His **offline practice site** and invented accounts mark a self-funded route unlike a workplace rotation.
He keeps **savings independent** of that project and conditions any later job search on displacement and paid openings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the thinking work in my developer role could go before there is a proved paid route elsewhere. A written notice period, funded training and actual support vacancies would help, along with rules keeping school records safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks where school login records go when a tool is used. I want someone at the company to answer that before we call any system safe. School login records should stay inside approved systems.

headlineQuote: School login records should stay inside approved systems.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old login software lead** with a master’s degree, high pay and about fourteen months of expenses saved.
He uses AI **occasionally on fake data** and waits for proof before adopting a method.
He wants **staff negotiations** over paid training and rules protecting school account records.
The **2028 scenario** alarms him because coding work could disappear despite strong savings and local options.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his developer role before another paid path is proven.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, company-funded training, real vacancies and safe school-data rules would ease a move.
